t: What Do We Talk About When We Talk About Performance? Dialogue Theory and Performance Budgeting
abs: This article examines the Program Assessment Rating Tool (PART) in the federal budgeting process. The early evidence on PART prompts the search for a theory of budgeting that accepts that performance information will influence decisions but will not be used in the same way from decision to decision, as the espoused theory of performance budgeting suggests. Dialogue theory emphasizes the ambiguity of performance information and related resource allocation choices. An exploratory test of dialogue theory is undertaken through an experiment involving graduate students assessing PART evaluations. The results illustrate a variety of ways in which different individuals can examine the same program and, using logical warrants, come to different conclusions about performance and future funding requirements.

t: Institutional Change and Coproduction of Public Services: The Effect of Charter Schools on Parental Involvement
abs: Recent discussions of school choice have revived arguments that the decentralization of governing institutions can enhance the quality of public services by increasing the participation of intended beneficiaries in the production of those services. We use data from the Schools and Staffing Survey to examine the extent to which the decentralization of authority to charter schools induces parents to become more involved in their children's schools. We find that parents are indeed more involved in charter schools than in observationally similar public schools, especially in urban elementary and middle schools. Although we find that this difference is partly attributable to measurable institutional and organizational factors, we also find that charter schools tend to be established in areas with above-average proportions of involved parents, and we find suggestive evidence that, within those areas, it is the more involved parents who tend to select into charter schools. Thus, while the institutional characteristics of charter schools do appear to induce parents to become more involved in their children's schools, such characteristics are only part of the explanation for the greater parental involvement in charter schools than in traditional public schools.

t: Sectoral Ethos: An Investigation of the Personal Values Systems of Female and Male Managers in the Public and Private Sectors
abs: The personal values systems of 884 public- and private-sector managers are compared. From that comparison inferences are drawn regarding the ethos of each sector, and potential implications for managers are discussed. Although the personal-values systems in the two sectors are quite similar, results reflect a public-sector ethos that is significantly higher in Delayed Gratification and Self-Expansion and a private-sector ethos that is significantly higher in Competence, Personal Orientation, and Family Security. In addition, this study furthers the view that the personal-values systems of male and female managers within a given employment sector are not significantly different.

t: Testing the Expectancy Disconfirmation Model of Citizen Satisfaction with Local Government
abs: It is important for public administration researchers and practitioners to understand how citizens form satisfaction judgments regarding local government services. A prior study by Van Ryzin (2004) found strong support for an expectancy disconfirmation model of citizen satisfaction, which focuses on the gap between performance and expectations. This model has been tested for decades in studies of private sector customer satisfaction, yet it is little known and applied in the field of public administration. The present study seeks to replicate the Van Ryzin (2004) results, which were based on a telephone survey in New York City, using a nationwide sample and a much different survey methodology, namely, an online, self-administered survey of a national panel. In addition, this study tests the sensitivity of the results to two alternative measures of disconfirmation (or the gap between performance and expectations). Results using subtractive disconfirmation confirm the basic expectancy disconfirmation model, but results using perceived disconfirmation do not, calling into question the policy and management implications of the prior study.

t: Administrative Responsiveness to the Disadvantaged: The Case of Children's Health Insurance
abs: Issues of administrative responsiveness to the disadvantaged (as distinct from formal policy responsiveness) possess important implications for American democracy. In this regard, the administrative practices that facilitate or impede enrollment, or take-up, in social programs deserve attention. This study focuses on two means-tested programs in the context of American federalism, Medicaid and the State Children's Health Insurance Program. Based on an in-depth analysis of seventeen states, we develop an index of administrative responsiveness to the disadvantaged related to take-up. We then explore some possible sources of variation in responsiveness rooted in the task environment, political ideology, good government culture and practice, and signals from political principals. Our findings point to the need to refine and expand upon existing explanations of state variation in social programs. Among other things, this study suggests the political importance of international (not interstate) population mobility and gubernatorial leadership (rather than bureaucratic autonomy) in shaping administrative responsiveness to the disadvantaged. It also points to the need for a contingent approach in examining whether the greater presence of racial minorities tends to depress such responsiveness.

t: New Public Management Is Dead--Long Live Digital-Era Governance
abs: The “new public management” (NPM) wave in public sector organizational change was founded on themes of disaggregation, competition, and incentivization. Although its effects are still working through in countries new to NPM, this wave has now largely stalled or been reversed in some key “leading-edge” countries. This ebbing chiefly reflects the cumulation of adverse indirect effects on citizens' capacities for solving social problems because NPM has radically increased institutional and policy complexity. The character of the post-NPM regime is currently being formed. We set out the case that a range of connected and information technology–centered changes will be critical for the current and next wave of change, and we focus on themes of reintegration, needs-based holism, and digitization changes. The overall movement incorporating these new shifts is toward “digital-era governance” (DEG), which involves reintegrating functions into the governmental sphere, adopting holistic and needs-oriented structures, and progressing digitalization of administrative processes. DEG offers a perhaps unique opportunity to create self-sustaining change, in a broad range of closely connected technological, organizational, cultural, and social effects. But there are alternative scenarios as to how far DEG will be recognized as a coherent phenomenon and implemented successfully.

t: Unleashing Social Psychology on Public Administration
abs: Steven Kelman served as the U.S. government's senior procurement policy official in the first Clinton administration. He assumed office anticipating “a better-than-even chance … nothing would improve” (83). To his surprise, he was able to lead frontline procurement employees to make significant reforms. After leaving office, Kelman then set out to explain why. Using the empirical methods of social psychology, he sought to understand how the troops came to buy into the message of reform he delivered. Unleashing Change is his answer. Kelman's main thesis in Unleashing Change is that a significant minority of frontline procurement staff was dissatisfied with the status quo and was looking for leadership that would empower the staff to do things differently. Once that leadership was provided, the change movement created sufficient positive feedback to convert the fence-sitters and skeptics. Kelman generalizes from this to argue that he has provided a new model of organizational change. He is explicitly critical of what he calls the guru literature, which asserts—based mainly on private sector experience—that people and organizations always resist change, that using or, if necessary, manufacturing a crisis (“the burning platform”) is the best way to trigger change, and that shock-and-awe tactics, such as firing the critics and bribing the skeptics, are essential to the implementation of change. I make two disclaimers. First, I am partial to Kelman's argument—in particular, his critique of the guru literature—because it accords with my own research on public management innovation. The narratives of champions of successful public management innovations demonstrate they were much more often proactively solving problems than reacting to crises, and their preferred implementation tactics were persuasion and accommodation rather than shock-and-awe (Borins 2001). Second, I have known Kelman since we were both undergraduates in the Social Studies program at Harvard. I believe this formative intellectual experience (which I shared) is reflected in this book. The primary methodology for Unleashing Change was survey research. Approximately a year after leaving office in 1997, Kelman conducted two surveys, a printed questionnaire for frontline procurement employees and semistructured in-person interviews with 272 frontline employees and senior local management. The questionnaire included approximately 500 questions about attitudes toward procurement reform, behavioral change as a result of reform, and personality and organizational context measures. Distributed at 19 buying offices, the survey yielded 1,600 replies. The core of the book is Kelman's analysis of a rich set of regressions: for example, structural equation models that explain underlying attitudes toward job autonomy—an important motive for reform—and ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions that explain, first, the difference between early and late support for change and, second, the effects of personality, demographic, and organizational variables on behavioral change. Overall, the regression analysis is impressive. Kelman masterfully operationalizes concepts drawn from social psychology, constructs and analyzes nonlinear and interaction effects, and breaks his large sample into informative subsamples. That said, I pose three questions regarding the analysis: methodological, presentational, and contextual. As its former senior official, Kelman received privileged access to the procurement community. Kelman's status likely explains why so many busy professionals were willing to complete so lengthy a questionnaire. Because Kelman did his research during the second Clinton administration, when his initiatives continued to have strong official endorsement, one might ask whether that disposed those completing his questionnaire or answering his in-person questions to tell him what they believed he wanted to hear. The book does not adequately answer the question of how he attempted to control for this potential source of bias. If the reader wants to follow the statistical analysis, it is essential that the regression equations be presented clearly. Kelman relegated definitions of variables to an appendix and some details about construction of the variables to footnotes. Given that the variables were often psychological scales from 1 to 5 or thermometers from 1 to 100, and the interpretation of endpoints differed from one variable to another, it was sometimes difficult and time-consuming to link the in-text analysis to the tables. A better approach would have been to present detailed definitions of variables close to the equations and also to display hypothesized signs of independent variables. My contextual concern stems from research of my own, undertaken long ago in the United States's northern neighbor, regarding bilingualism in air traffic control (Borins 1983). Essentially, what was at issue was whether to introduce the use of French into the air traffic control system in the predominantly francophone province of Quebec. The question arose in the early 1970s when private and recreational pilots who were more comfortable using French than English and bilingual francophone controllers, who could readily serve francophone pilots in French, challenged what until then had been a system conducted completely in English. In 1975 the government headed by Pierre Trudeau decided to accommodate francophone controllers and pilots, and so “unleashed change.” It also unleashed a vociferous backlash on the part of unilingual anglophone controllers working in, and pilots flying over, Quebec. The opponents to change effectively exploited the collective bargaining process and the fear in English Canada that the imposition of bilingualism would jeopardize public safety. Ultimately, the francophones had their way, but only after the unilingual anglophone controllers received a generous relocation package and the government conducted elaborate laboratory simulations showing that a bilingual system could be made as safe as a unilingual one. A case like this, involving a workforce that embodies a society's most divisive cleavage, stands as a polar opposite to Kelman's. If Kelman is to use his case to develop a general theory of unleashing change, he must also consider cases where unleashing change also unleashes concerted resistance to change and attempt to describe points along a continuum between them. The Harvard Social Studies program, to which I referred at the outset, is an interdisciplinary social sciences program that begins with the study of the greats who inspired modern social science—Marx, Freud, Durkheim, Weber—and then lets loose its students to make sense of modern political science, economics, sociology, and anthropology. Entry to the program was limited, and for serious social science students at Harvard three decades ago, it was the place to be. (Among the thirty-five graduates in my year, the most prominent in public life in the United States are Senator Charles Schumer, University of Pennsylvania president Amy Gutmann, and Harvard law professor Lani Guinier.) The influence of Social Studies on Unleashing Change is clear. Public administration is an applied field that has always drawn on the core social science disciplines, initially political science and more recently economics. Kelman's work is rooted in social psychology, and he is the first public administration scholar to apply its methodologies in a sustained and rigorous way. Still, he has not ignored political science, notably in his application of organizational politics to the dynamics of bureaucratic change, and he uses microeconomics to analyze incentives to change individual behavior. Kelman also draws on more distant sources, such as Schama on the French Revolution, Walzer on the exodus from Egypt, and Lenin on the Russian Revolution. These references are not intellectual showmanship; they broaden Kelman's argument materially and convincingly. Unleashing Change has just been published at the start of George W. Bush's second administration. This raises the question of what it would have looked like had Kelman chosen to publish sooner, using traditional public administration methodology. He would likely have drawn more from his own experience, conducted far fewer interviews, and published midway through the second Clinton administration. Such a book would have paid more attention to the procurement legislation Kelman championed: the Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act of 1994 and the Federal Acquisition Reform Act of 1995, both of which are dealt with in a mere two pages (136–37). In general, the hypothetical book would have put more emphasis on upward relationships with the White House and Congress. It would also likely have included a chapter on the results achieved by procurement reform—faster acquisition, lower prices, and better value—an unfortunate absence in Unleashing Change. Kelman would likely defend his approach by arguing that his experience as a senior bureaucratic player (Allison's Model III) is of less theoretical and practical significance than that of frontline and middle-level procurement staff (Allison's Model II). There is an analogy here with the evolution of traditional history, which focused on leadership, legislation, and diplomacy, to modern history, which pays much more attention to the lives of ordinary workers and families. In the last chapter of the book he did write, Kelman reports that the first administrator of the Office of Federal Procurement Policy under Bush instituted a “back to basics” procurement policy, reverting to the traditional concern about controlling abuse. Perhaps a stronger statement by Kelman years earlier might have prevented this shifting of course. Much of the second half of Kelman's book is concerned with maintaining support for reform among the procurement community, but there is no mention of maintaining political support in the event of a change in the governing party. Given the frequent alternation of power between Democrats and Republicans, reformers in relatively nonideological areas such as procurement should think about how to maintain progress on a bipartisan basis. The process of writing Unleashing Change makes clear the nature of the accomplishment. Before then, Kelman was primarily a qualitative political scientist. To write this book, he familiarized himself with a vast literature in social psychology and, with the help of colleagues and research assistants, taught himself the necessary statistics. Learning a new literature and what is essentially a new language at this stage in a career involves a major commitment. Writing this book took seven years and was Kelman's major focus during that time. Public administration schools appear to be taking the lead from business schools in giving faculty strong incentives to write articles for top-tier journals because that improves the schools' rankings. I hope our profession, remembering its roots in political science, will retain its commitment to making the greater investment of time necessary to write books—as good as this one. The endorsement by Roderick Kramer, of the Stanford business school, for Unleashing Change calls the book “an analytic tour de force.” I agree completely. Thus, I am confident that public administration scholars will read it for many years to come. But what will its impact be? Will it achieve Kelman's aim of “mainstreaming public administration and public management research” (36) by encouraging social psychologists to turn their attention to the public sector? Will it stimulate public administration researchers to look more deeply at the dynamics of bureaucratic change at the front lines? Will it lead public administration researchers to contribute to the mainstream social psychology journals (for example, Journal of Applied Psychology) that Kelman frequently cites? To ask these questions is itself to acknowledge the magnitude of Kelman's achievement.

t: Agencies: Arm's-Length Government within Easy Reach?
abs: This book explores the phenomenon of “agencies,” defined by these authors as public bodies that are semi-autonomous, but not formally independent of traditional ministerial departments, and that carry out activities on behalf of those departments. While the use of agencies (sometimes termed “executive agencies”) is not new, as this timely book argues, they have become more significant in many countries as part of the “New Public Management”—for example, in the creation of “Next Steps” executive agencies in the United Kingdom (U.K.), Special Operating Agencies in Canada, Agentschappen in the Netherlands, and Independent Administrative Corporations in Japan. Agencies reports the findings of the first major comparative study of the agency phenomenon and forms part of a small but growing literature on the distinctive issues raised by this form of public organization. In particular, the issues are closely related but are not the same as those raised by public bodies with more formal independence from ministerial departments, such as organizations often called “quangos”; staff members in agencies are often much less confident about the autonomy of their own activities and need to have much greater sensitivity to departmental concerns. From the other direction, agencies are different from traditional integrated departmental structures, where the chain of command tends to be (but is not always!) a bit clearer and bureaucrats' obligations to direct reporting and response to executive politicians are stronger. This book on agencies sits within a portfolio of work by the authors on broader public management reforms, which also examines these other types of body (Pollitt and Bouckaert 2004; Pollitt and Talbot 2004).

t: Bureaucracy and Democracy: A Happy Marriage?
abs: Bureaucracy is a significant element of American governance; yet, its role in democratic governance is all too often vilified, misunderstood, and reduced to stereotypical assumptions that fail to recognize the contributions of bureaucratic structures and actors in the design and implementation of public policy. These misguided assumptions and underestimations of public sector bureaucracy, therefore, require practical and empirical examples that run contrary to the current political environment and managerial reform efforts that typically adopt simple slogans as paradigms: “cutting the fat,” “reducing red tape for results,” “adopting private sector efficiencies.” These are only the most recent versions of simple assumptions that have handicapped government since at least the late nineteenth century. William T. Gormley, Jr. and Steven J. Balla's book offers a thoughtful and practical counterpoint—a very useful analysis with extensive examples that provide insights on the realities of implementing complex public policies. The authors aim to dispel myths about bureaucracy by drawing on examples that highlight bureaucratic responsiveness, capacity for significant reform, and the use of discretion to improve conditions for individuals and organizations throughout society. As bureaucracy and accountability are the focus of this book, Gormley and Balla describe how bureaucracy is accoun , to whom, under what circumstances, and for which results. Insights are drawn from several disciplines and from empirical research that illuminates bureaucracy's complex external environment. The authors' presentation of management techniques and concepts provides rich details as to the interior dynamics of public agencies.

t: Dramatic Reform in the Public Service: At-Will Employment and the Creation of a New Public Workforce
abs: As is widely known, the state of Georgia transformed its civil service system in the mid-1990s. A new performance management and pay-for-performance plan was put into place, and authority for personnel policy was significantly decentralized, but perhaps most notably, all employees hired or promoted after July 1, 1996, were placed in the state's unclassified service where they were required to serve on an at-will basis. In stark contrast, state workers hired into their positions earlier continued to enjoy an array of job protections and appeals rights as members of the traditional classified service. This article seeks to understand the impact of such dramatic public service reform on the attitudes of employees. A survey of unclassified (at-will) and classified employees conducted four years after the reforms revealed generally negative views toward the array of changes in the state's personnel policies, but interestingly, unclassified employees were significantly less negative about the full range of reforms than their classified co-workers, even when differences in age, tenure, and other factors were held constant.

t: Taking Tough Choices Seriously: Public Administration and Individual Moral Agency
abs: Using the concepts of thick and thin relationships as the basis for ethical behavior, this paper critiques the emphasis on discretion in the mainstream administrative ethics literature and argues that moral and other dilemmas facing public administrators provide a more useful frame. Two examples drawn from the UK Hutton Investigation into the death of David Kelly are used to demonstrate the relevance and usefulness of this approach.

t: Taking Initiative: Proactive Management and Organizational Performance in Networked Environments
abs: While current research in network management focuses on establishing, empirically, that network management contributes positively to organizational performance, theoretical work remains to answer how network management induces positive organizational outcomes. Similarly, although the classical intraorganizational management perspective may seem unsuitable for today's multiorganizational environment, researchers should not abandon what classic organizational theory can offer as the perspective continues to shift. This article represents a first step toward bringing a proactive management perspective to bear on the empirical analysis of managerial activity and program performance, when operating within a networked environment. The goal is to enable researchers to see a clearer picture of how network management, particularly proactive management, influences organizational performance on a set of programmatic indicators. Public education provides the context for the investigation.

t: Managing Stakeholder Involvement in Decision Making: A Comparative Analysis of Six Interactive Processes in the Netherlands
abs: Initiatives to encourage and stimulate the involvement of citizens but also various societal organizations in decision making can be seen in a wide variety of European countries. Citizen panels, citizen charters, new types of participation, and other forms are being used to increase the influence of citizens on decision making and to improve the relation between citizens and elected politicians. In the Netherlands a lot of local governments have experimented with interactive decision making that is enhancing the influence of citizens and interest groups on public policy making. The main motives to involve stakeholders in interactive decision making are to diminish the veto power of various societal actors by involving them in decision making, improve the quality of decision making by using the information and solutions of various actors, and bridge the perceived growing cleavage between citizens and elected politicians. In this article six cases are evaluated. The cases are compared on three dimensions: the nature and organization of participation, the way the process is managed (process management), and the relation with formal democratic institutions. These organizational features (in terms of both formal organization and actual performance) are compared with the results of the decision-making processes in the six cases. The article shows that the high expectations of interactive decision making are not always met. It also shows that managing the interactions—called process management in network theory—is very important for achieving satisfactory outcomes.

t: Interests and Implementation: Fostering Voluntary Regulatory Actions
abs: This research addresses the role of interest groups in the implementation of voluntary forms of regulation to prevent harms to water quality. Voluntary programs engender information uncertainties and competing pressures on decisions to address potential harms. We address hypotheses about these considerations for data about actions undertaken by marine facilities, with particular attention to differences in the influence of governmental actors, environmental groups, and trade associations. We find that these influences are shaped to differing degrees by the trust placed in information sources, fears of future regulation, a sense of duty to act, and desire to reduce informational and regulatory uncertainties. These findings suggest potential roles for interest groups in overcoming information gaps in the implementation of voluntary regulatory programs.

t: Accounting for the Value of Performance Measurement from the Perspective of Midwestern Mayors
abs: This article studies the decades-long question, “Does performance measurement matter?” by examining how and why Midwest mayors perceive value in performance measurement. The results show that the tool is perceived positively, but its impact on decision making depends on whether performance measurement is integrated into strategic planning, goal setting, and internal communication between city council members and departmental staff and on whether major stakeholders are involved in developing performance measures. The article discusses the implications for future results-oriented reforms and concludes that simply reporting performance information in budgetary or public documents is not enough. Rather, a more comprehensive look at the implementation issues of performance measurement and performance budgeting is necessary.

t: Governing the Quango: An Auditing and Cheating Model of Quasi-Governmental Authorities
abs: The New Public Management has a paramount implication for the delegation of authority to implement public policy, namely, that efficient delegations are designed according to the substance of the task to be performed. In other words, the government must be able to choose the best agent to carry out a particular task, which implies that the set of agents must not be confined to actors and departments within the bureaucracy. This flexibility of form creates the incentives behind the quango, and increases the importance of ex ante design for the legislature to avoid misuse of public funds. It also has the potential to increase ex post enforcement activity by the government. This article examines ex ante design from the perspective of auditing, presenting a formal model of the construction of auditing procedures as a response to expectations of the misuse of funds. By creating requirements such as the requisite submission of annual plans, reports, and accounts, governments attempt to create a compliance-inducing scheme much like that present in tax enforcement. The theoretical model generates empirical predictions that are statistically examined using data on public bodies in the Netherlands created between 1946 and 1993. Empirical results demonstrate strong support for the theory.

t: Performance Management in Practice: A Comparative Study of Executive Agencies
abs: This article reports a study of performance management practices in four functions across four European Union member states (Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden, and the United Kingdom). The focus is on how and to what extent performance indicators influenced the top management of the agencies concerned and the degree to which performance data were used by ministries as steering instruments. The research uses a historical institutionalist perspective combined with a model that identifies primary task characteristics as a source of significant variation. Thus the design explores both the influence of task characteristics (through contrasts among the four different functions) and embedded national system characteristics (through contrasts among the four countries). I show that both primary task characteristics and national system characteristics had some of the theoretically predicted effects on the management regimes. Equally, however, certain general tendencies embraced all countries and most functions. These include, first, the incremental growth of more sophisticated performance indicator systems and, second, the feebleness of ministries in developing performance-based strategic steering.

t: Casework Job Design and Client Outcomes in Welfare-to-Work Offices
abs: Differences in performance across different locations of a human service program may be driven by client, managerial, organizational, policy, or environmental characteristics. While many of these factors are outside the control of local managers, other factors may be open to influence by local discretion and may have independent effects on performance. One issue facing local managers is how to divide job tasks among frontline staff, but little evidence is available regarding whether job design is related to performance. In this article, I examine the relationships between different casework task configurations and welfare-to-work office performance. Controlling for a number of client and office characteristics, I find that clients' average earnings are higher over a two-year period in offices that primarily use unified case management and in offices with a specialist who develops job opportunities. I find no effects on earnings in offices that use other kinds of specialists and no effects of unified case management or specialists on welfare benefit receipt in the two-year period. Overall, the findings suggest that local managerial decisions regarding job design help explain the variation in performance across offices and suggest a possible lever through which performance can be improved.

t: Regulation in the States
abs: At the very moment that state regulatory powers are being extended in new ways in numerous areas of public policy, Paul Teske offers the most comprehensive analysis of the evolving state government role published to date. Much as James Q. Wilson assembled an impressive team of young scholars to explore federal regulatory policy a quarter century ago in The Politics of Regulation, Teske has gathered an outstanding collection of former graduate students to offer a penetrating look at the ways in which state governments tackle a wide range of regulatory tasks. This is a sobering undertaking, attempting broad generalization about state governance as well as detailed analysis of nine distinct issue areas, ranging from telecommunications, to hospital expansion, to groundwater protection. As Teske notes, the sheer scope of state government involvement in regulatory affairs is staggering: states provide direct regulation of approximately 20 percent of the economy (10), state legislatures collectively generate seventy-five times more legislation than Congress does (200), and approximately 37,000 lobbying organizations were in operation in respective state capitals as recently as 2000 (203). Indeed, Teske quickly sets to rest the periodic assertions throughout American political history that state government roles in regulation were destined to decline, because of either deregulation or the usurpation of those roles by the federal government.

t: Comparing Public and Private Sector Decision-Making Practices
abs: Public and private sector decision making is studied with an experiment. The study compares decision making in a tax-supported general purpose governmental agency with that done by a business firm selling to a market, using a simulation to capture differences in the preferences and practices of mid-level managers working in the two sectors. The simulation calls for participating managers to assess the risk and prospect of adopting budgets tailored to match each sector. A cognitive culture that stresses analysis, speculation, bargaining, or networking is employed to fashion a budget appropriate for a public and a private sector organization, each with a controversial and a noncontroversial budget amount. The literature on public/private differences was consulted to make predictions, suggesting that public sector managers would favor bargaining and networking and private sector managers would favor analysis and speculation. The cognitive style literature suggests that managers favor budgets constructed with an approach that is consistent with their preferred cognitive style and see less risk in the choice, except in a public setting where risk would be unaffected. The study finds that private sector managers are more apt to support budget decisions made with analysis and less likely to support them when bargaining is applied. Public sector managers are less likely to support budget decisions backed by analysis and more likely to support those that are derived from bargaining with agency people.

t: Assessing Performance Budgeting at OMB: The Influence of Politics, Performance, and Program Size
abs: This article investigates the impact of performance, as measured by the OMB performance budgeting initiative called Performance Assessment Rating Tool (PART), on recommendations in the President's budget. In a multivariate analysis using data from the FY 2005 budget, with appropriate controls for the political content of programs, we find that the PART scores have a statistically significant impact on budget decisions within OMB. We find that PART scores have a larger impact on small and medium sized programs than on large programs. We also find that the “results” component of PART scores has a smaller impact on budget decisions than the “program purpose” component, a finding which tends to contradict the goal of performance budgeting to redirect resources to programs that produce results. The relative unimportance of the “results” component may be due to the lack of good outcome measures for most programs in PART.

t: Sweet-Talking the Fourth Branch: The Influence of Interest Group Comments on Federal Agency Rulemaking
abs: Students of politics have identified a variety of actors who appear to influence the federal bureaucracy's implementation of public policy, including Congress, the president, and interest groups. These lines of research, however, have often portrayed interest groups as actors with indirect influence (who, for example, work through or with Congress), rather than assessing the direct influence of interest groups on bureaucratic policy outputs. I conduct a test of direct interest group influence by analyzing an original data set composed of 1,444 interest group comments in reaction to forty federal agency rules. I find, contrary to the expectations of the extant literature, that the formal participation of interest groups during rulemaking can, and often does, alter the content of policy within the “fourth branch” of government. I conclude that those who voice their preferences during the notice and comment period rulemaking are often able to change government policy outputs to better match their preferences.

t: Diversity, Representation, and Performance: Evidence about Race and Ethnicity in Public Organizations
abs: In the past twenty years, the growing percentages of racial and ethnic minorities in the United States have led scholars to pay increased attention to the issue of diversity. However, very little research using the public organization as the unit of analysis has sought to understand the true impact of workforce diversity on work-related outcomes. This study seeks to understand the impact of one type of diversity—race and ethnicity—on organizational outcomes in public education. Using data from Texas public school districts, the article finds that diversity among managers is unrelated to the three performance outcomes tested, while diversity among teachers is negatively related to one and positively related to two performance outcomes. Representation among managers, on the other hand, is positively related to all three performance outcomes, while representation of teachers is negatively related to one of the outcomes.

t: Casting Light on Shadow Government: A Typological Approach
abs: Our fascination with the growth of special purpose entities has garnered substantial theoretical and empirical attention in the last several decades. Unfortunately, we still know very little about the unique characteristics of various special purpose entities. Our lack of understanding regarding special purpose entities has contributed to both their categorization as “shadow government” and a tendency for distinct types of special purpose entities to be generalized. The resulting perception is that the terms “public authorities,” “special districts,” “government corporations,” and the like are interchangeable or synonymous. Because accurate understanding is necessary to achieve precise evaluation, this article explores the theoretical underpinnings of these complex entities and offers a typology based on these theories. The typology is then compared to the extant literature and individual special purpose entities.

t: Goo-Goos in Paradise
abs: What can government do to make welfare reform—or, for that matter, any significant policy change—work? Ours is an age when a poisonous skepticism toward government has become commonplace, fueled by the cynical maneuverings of an administration that has cut taxes and savagely excoriated government with one hand while vastly expanding government's reach and scope (think of the Department of Homeland Security, for example, or the extravagant expansion of Medicare) with the other. One oft-repeated but probably apocryphal anecdote neatly sums up the odd mixture of fear, loathing, expectation, and misunderstanding that Americans feel toward their government—what James Morone (1990, 1) has called “a dread and a yearning.” During the 1996 campaign, in the wake of President Bill Clinton's failed bid to reform the cockeyed American health care system, one frantic elderly citizen allegedly cornered a congressional candidate and begged, “Please, don't let the government take over my Medicare!” At such a moment, this question about the possibilities and promise of the public sector takes on particular urgency. The challenge of sorting out what government can and cannot do well and of considering how government can most effectively fulfill its democratic commitments must be considered one of the highest tasks of the policy sciences (Mettler and Soss 2004). It is this question that animates these three books, each of which seeks to explain some aspect of the role of public administration in welfare reform and its consequences in both the United States and the United Kingdom. The story of welfare reform, or of any significant policy development, is typically told as a tale in which politics—of the electoral, representative, interest-group variety—makes policy, meaning, primarily, laws. These laws, which usually represent the culmination of years of feverish activity by the policy system, then somehow result in some change in the state of the world that usually fails to measure up to the hopes and expectations of various actors who were behind the change in the first place. Analytically, this version of the policy story generally starts with the adoption of some kind of policy innovation or reform (which is rooted in the politics of ideas, interests, and institutions) and then leaps to the outcomes it produces, as if the role of the government is just to pass the law and not actually to implement it. The mechanics of this transformation of policy decisions into real-world outcomes remains one of the “black boxes” of policy studies, and each of these three works admirably attempts to open it and take a look inside. How can government best be organized to do the things that it, and often only it, is equipped to do? As a corollary, what is the appropriate role of the market, the profit motive, and the private sector in this activity? And what of the third sector, such as foundations, nonprofit service providers, and the other kinds of nongovernmental organizations that have so proliferated in recent years? What is the role of knowledge and expertise in these processes, and in which sector can that knowledge be most profitably located and most effectively exploited? Such questions surface with some regularity in American politics. For example, the 9/11 Commission has laid the failure to prevent the 2001 terrorist attacks on New York and Washington squarely at the feet not of the usual suspects: incompetence, ignorance, malfeasance, corruption, or partisanship. No, this time the culprits seem to be administrative mishaps and misorganization. In response, the president and his reelection challenger, in a characteristic game of electoral one-upmanship, resolutely and inspiringly pledged to reorganize the national intelligence services. The reorganization that was the product of this morality play will doubtless be blamed for the next calamitous intelligence failure and rearranged again, and so on down into the endless future. So this seems a reasonable time to take stock and ask just how do government and its performance matter in making policy work? What, in short, makes for good government? The aspiration for good government is an ancient one with an honorable lineage of theory and practice. In the United States of the twenty-first century, however, the possibility of “good government” remains, for many, a chimera and the quest after it a quixotic act, worthy only of derision. This cast of mind dates back at least to Theodore Roosevelt, who coined the term “goo-goo” to refer contemptuously to the prissy and moralistic Progressive reformers who he felt lacked the stomach and the backbone (and probably other body parts unsuitable for naming in a respectable publication) to carry out the rough work of government. Goo-gooism is itself a long and distinguished American tradition, stretching from the Mugwumps, muckrakers, and municipal reformers of the Progressive Era to organizations such as Common Cause and figures such as Al Gore and Ralph Nader today. Goo-goos are themselves a disparate group, but they are united by at least three characteristics. The first is a cultural sensibility. Goo-gooism was originally rooted in the norms and privileges of the native-born WASP elite who found its dominance of American politics, culture, and society under threat in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries by an unsettling and disorderly array of outsiders, namely, immigrants, workers, and the urban masses. This elite sought to manage the challenges of industrialism and urbanization, which threatened convulsive change to their well-ordered world, and to forestall the rise of socialism. Goo-gooism remains an elite phenomenon in the United States, rooted no longer in the sensibilities of a social class but in the new elite of the American educational and economic meritocracy and largely shorn of its nativist and racist trappings—although not always, as the meretricious work of Charles Murray has shown (Lemann 2000; Herrnstein and Murray 1994). Second, goo-goos share a near-absolute faith in expertise as the proper basis for the conduct of public affairs and in knowledge as a cure-all for social ills. The modern social sciences emerged in the late nineteenth century as essentially the R&D department of the burgeoning goo-goo movement. Their practitioners hoped to expose social problems and find remedies for them. And so arose the characteristic goo-goo forms: expert panels, independent commissions, legislative reference bureaus that were deliberately kept at arm's length from the rough-and-tumble of electoral politics, which was largely peopled by the very sort of folks that the goo-goos particularly feared and mistrusted. This approach to policy led almost inexorably to a sort of Rousseauian paternalism toward the benighted lower orders, who had to be protected from their own vicious tendencies and saved from their own choices. (To his credit, Lawrence Mead [1997], one of the authors under review here, does not shrink from the paternalistic implications of his own approach to policy and government.) Finally, goo-goos generally share a mistrust of politics that borders on contempt. Goo-gooism is rooted in the antimachine reform politics of the Progressive Era and hence tends to view the vote-seeking behavior of politicians as a hindrance to sound and effective public policies rather than as a potential vehicle for bringing them about. Goo-goos are thus typically made profoundly uncomfortable by lavish displays of self-interest, ambition, acquisitiveness, or power—in short, precisely the things that make democratic politics and capitalist markets work. These three characteristics highlight not only the weaknesses but also the strengths of the good government tradition. For the most part, goo-goos have always been motivated by a genuine passion for identifying and addressing social problems and, unlike many of the denizens of today's policy world of think tanks and partisan “research” outfits, have generally believed in the possibilities of government. The goo-goo tradition has been responsible for real advances in social knowledge. At the same time, this conviction and intelligence have often been undercut by narrow vision and limited imagination about not only the inescapability but also the possibilities of democratic politics. All of these goo-gooish tendencies are on display in these three books. Penny Leonard investigates the provision of information about social services to potential clients in the British welfare state, arguing sensibly that information is a critical component of social citizenship. In other words, people must know what their rights are in order to exercise them. In some spheres of public policy, this is an entirely commonplace observation. Anyone who has ever watched an American crime drama has seen a police officer bark out the famous Miranda formula to a cursing suspect: “You have the right to remain silent ….” Leonard's key insight is to suggest that what holds true for civil rights, such as the rights of a criminal suspect, should also hold true for social rights. When the state creates a social benefit, it may have an affirmative obligation to make every effort to ensure that potential beneficiaries know that they can claim it: “You have the right to remain solvent ….” Social benefits are not self-executing. It follows that the information infrastructure, the means by which the state seeks to inform potential beneficiaries of their rights, becomes a problematic and variable linkage mechanism between the state and citizens, whose very status as full citizens depends on their capacity to make claims. Leonard demonstrates some important sources of variation, across policies and over time, in the British welfare state's capacity and inclination to provide information to those citizens lower down the food chain (there's that pesky elite goo-goo sensibility) about the rights they have. Her most important finding is that the provision of information about social benefits seems to vary with the ideological nature of the government. Labour governments seem to be more forthcoming with information, while Conservative governments tend to be stingier. Right- and left-leaning governments seem to want different things out of existing welfare programs and apparently adjust information policy—resources invested, definition of the target audience, means of reaching that audience, and so forth—accordingly. This is certainly an interesting and revealing finding, and Leonard presents compelling evidence that governments self-consciously use information as a tool in the service of political objectives. But at the same time, this is not exactly a shocking finding, except perhaps to a goo-goo, for whom political motivations are generally considered suspect at best, and Leonard's narrative is shot through with this sensibility. There is fascinating material here, and Leonard deserves credit for combing carefully through a variety of primary and secondary sources to construct a convincing narrative of government's failure to live up to its information obligations. But the narrative tends to assume that “politics” is a relatively monolithic and undifferentiated sphere that is, by its very nature, inimical to good government. Political motives, Leonard writes in a rather circular way, “can be summarised as promoting political values and goals, as enhancing political legitimacy and image, and as political pragmatism and expediency…. ‘Political’ motives may also further vested interests, either promoting a particular policy for personal reasons or for career advancement” (118). Not a word about, say, representation or electoral competition over scarce resources and divergent values, also important functions of democratic politics, whose role is to ensure that policy outcomes bear some relation to the interests and preferences of citizens. The next step, for which Leonard has ably paved the way, will be to transcend the limitations of the goo-goo sensibility to build an inquiry about how political conflicts and structures systematically affect the government's capacity and propensity to inform its citizens, an investigation that is, at least at the outset, more neutral toward democratic politics as an essential component of the policy process. M. Bryna Sanger does not so much disparage politics as sidestep it altogether as an important element of the process of implementing welfare reform. She investigates the means of delivering employment and training services under welfare reform at the local level. In particular, she probes the tension among the public, private, and nonprofit sectors as direct providers, and she highlights the comparative risks and rewards of each approach. Through a comparative examination of reform implementation in Houston, Milwaukee, New York City, and San Diego, she adds cogently and effectively to the growing chorus of skepticism about the benefits of privatization. Contracting welfare services out, whether to for-profit firms or nonprofit organizations, she concludes, actually requires more rather than less government oversight and expertise because of the monitoring costs involved in supervising an agent rather than doing the work directly. All of this Sanger shows quite effectively through acutely observed and carefully drawn portraits of both the common challenges and idiosyncrasies of the process of implementing welfare reform in each city. But Sanger does not get all she could out of this fascinating material, and especially out of the potential for comparison across cities as a way of making general inferences about the factors that might affect the success of competitive contracting of welfare services in a variety of settings. Above all, politics is strangely absent from her story. There is little about the political structures and forces that affect the decisions of mayors and other government officials, private contractors and the bureaucrats who manage them, advocacy groups, and other actors who shape the conduct of public affairs. As a case in point, New York City is one of Sanger's cases, but Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, the dominant figure on the city's political and policy scene, makes only one appearance, as does Jason Turner, his welfare commissioner, fresh from his star turn on the Wisconsin welfare reform stage (which Mead chronicles). Sanger's brand of goo-gooism differs somewhat from Leonard's in that Sanger's analysis displays not so much anxiety about politics as indifference to it. But both share the goo-gooish presumption that successful governance is a technical matter best left beyond the reach of politicians. Mead's goo-gooism, by contrast, is of a rather different stripe. He does not share the deep skepticism of politics or the conviction that politics and governance are (or should be) separate spheres. But what he lacks in politics-anxiety he more than makes up for elsewhere, particularly in his faith in elite judgments and the importance of very particular cultural values. Mead's book is an extraordinary chronicle of perhaps the most well known and successful instance of American welfare reform in the 1990s, in Wisconsin. Through a judicious combination of interviews, participant-observation, documentary research, and statistical analysis, Mead tells the remarkable story of Wisconsin Works, the pioneering work-based program that predated and prefigured the 1996 national welfare reform. His purpose is to explain why Wisconsin apparently succeeded, and outperformed other states, in reducing its cash-assistance rolls, moving former welfare recipients into jobs, and on the whole improving their standard of living. His answer is governmental excellence. More than other states, he argues, “Wisconsin derived a good government from its past, used it to craft the best policies known at the time, and obtained good results from them” (14). The two key steps in Mead's causal chain are, first, the assertion that governmental excellence was the critical causal factor that led Wisconsin to adopt particular policies and to see them through effectively and, second, that it was Wisconsin's distinctive, historically rooted political culture that the state to have good government in the first place. t: Multiple Public Service Performance Indicators: Toward an Integrated Statistical Approach
abs: Public service organizations usually produce multiple outputs, measured on different scales, giving rise to a suite of performance indicators. The traditional approach to statistical analysis of organizational performance has been to develop a separate regression model for each performance indicator. This piecemeal approach, the article argues, may discard valuable information, as it ignores potentially important relationships between individual performance measures. We therefore propose modeling an organization's performance measures simultaneously, using the methods of seemingly unrelated regressions. The approach implicitly introduces a latent organizational variable into the regressions and may therefore economize on the need to assemble explicit measures of organizational characteristics. The method is illustrated using an example from English public hospitals.

t: Maybe It Is Time to Rediscover Bureaucracy
abs: This article questions the fashionable ideas that bureaucratic organization is an obsolescent, undesirable, and non-viable form of administration and that there is an inevitable and irreversible paradigmatic shift towards market- or network-organization. In contrast, the paper argues that contemporary democracies are involved in another round in a perennial debate and ideological struggle over what are desirable forms of administration and government: that is, a struggle over institutional identities and institutional balances. The argument is not that bureaucratic organization is a panacea and the answer to all challenges of public administration. Rather, bureaucratic organization is part of a repertoire of overlapping, supplementary, and competing forms coexisting in contemporary democracies, and so are market-organization and network-organization. Rediscovering Weber's analysis of bureaucratic organization, then, enriches our understanding of public administration. This is in particular true when we (a) include bureaucracy as an institution, not only an instrument; (b) look at the empirical studies in their time and context, not only at Weber's ideal-types and predictions; and (c) take into account the political and normative order bureaucracy is part of, not only the internal characteristics of “the bureau.”

t: Goal Ambiguity and Organizational Performance in U.S. Federal Agencies
abs: In spite of numerous observations that government organizations have high levels of organizational goal ambiguity that exert major influences on their other characteristics, few researchers have measured goal ambiguity and tested these frequent assertions. In previous research, we developed measures of four dimensions of goal ambiguity: mission comprehension ambiguity, directive goal ambiguity, evaluative goal ambiguity, and priority goal ambiguity. Confirming hypotheses developed from the literature on public organizations, the latter three variables showed relations to such organizational characteristics as organizational age, financial publicness (proportion of funding from government allocations), and regulatory status. This article reports a second analytical step of examining the relations between the goal ambiguity dimensions and indicators of organizational performance based on responses to the 2000 National Partnership for Reinventing Government Survey of federal employees. The performance variables included managerial effectiveness, customer service orientation, productivity, and work quality. Regression analyses with numerous control variables found that directive, evaluative, and priority goal ambiguity related negatively to managerial effectiveness. All four performance indicators showed significant negative relationships with evaluative goal ambiguity and directive goal ambiguity. The results provide further evidence of the viability of the new measures of goal ambiguity, support theory-based but previously untested hypotheses, and further indicate the feasibility and value of analyzing goal ambiguity of government organizations.

t: In the Eye of the Storm: Frontline Supervisors and Federal Agency Performance
abs: This study examines the role of frontline supervisors in the twenty-two largest federal agencies and explores their contributions to organizational performance and effectiveness. Specifically, this study develops a measure of federal agency performance and tests a hybrid model that predicts it. Several research questions on the nature and importance of supervisory management are tested within this framework. Data for the study come from the 2000 Merit Principles Survey, U.S. Merit Systems Protection Board. The findings show that “management matters.” Frontline supervisors play an important role in organizational performance and effectiveness, and supervisory management is an important determinant of high performance in federal agencies. In addition, high-performing agencies tend to have skillful upper-level managers, strong cultures that value employees and emphasize the importance and meaningfulness of the agency's work, and policies that empower those employees. These agencies also tend to have a strong performance orientation, and they strive for workforce diversity. These findings are explained further, and their implications are discussed.

t: Introducing the "Determinants of Performance in Public Organizations" Symposium
abs: The performance of public organizations has become a topic of great interest to scholars and practitioners of public management around the globe. This interest stems from theoretical and methodological puzzles posed by organizational performance. This is not just an academic endeavor—the desire of politicians to improve public services has become more important over recent years. In the United Kingdom the Labour government has published and implemented a Public Service Improvement strategy (Office of Public Service Reform 2002), while the U.S. federal government's National Performance Review and Government Performance Results Act 1993 from the Clinton administration through to George W. Bush's President's Management Agenda have sought higher levels of performance from government. Recently, the Chinese government has published an index of measures to evaluate the performance of Chinese cities (China Daily 2004). The interest in performance also reflects the need for public organizations to cope with emergency events, such as the terrorist attacks of 9/11, the health epidemics of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome and bird flu in the Far East, and the tsunami that swept across the Indian Ocean at Christmas 2004.

t: Representative Bureaucracy, Organizational Strategy, and Public Service Performance: An Empirical Analysis of English Local Government
abs: The theory of representative bureaucracy suggests that organizations perform better if their workforces reflect the characteristics of their constituent populations. The management literature implies that the impact of representative bureaucracy is contingent on organizational strategy. Our empirical evidence on English local government is inconsistent with the basic theory of representative bureaucracy but supports a moderating effect of organizational strategy. Representative bureaucracy is negatively associated with citizens' perceptions of local authority performance. However, organizations pursuing a prospector strategy are able to mitigate this negative relationship.

t: Where Next? Research Directions on Performance in Public Organizations
abs: The dependent variable in all the articles presented in this symposium issue of JPART was organizational performance in public agencies. Management variables included organizational strategy, resources, leadership, goals, workforce diversity, and representation. The empirical articles also controlled for external effects on performance. Although the collection of articles presented here is a major step forward for research on public organizations, the evidence that management matters needs additional exploration, and the methods used by scholars need to be improved. Public organizations are required to address a range of goals, some of which may be in conflict. This obligation in turn requires organizations that deliver public services to focus their attention on multiple dimensions of performance. Boyne (2002) has identified sixteen dimensions of performance in public organizations grouped into five themes—outputs, efficiency, effectiveness, responsiveness, and democratic outcomes. Four of these themes are captured in the empirical articles presented here. Output quality is considered by Andrews et al., Brewer, Chun and Rainey, and Martin and Smith, while output quantity features in the study by Andrews et al.1 Efficiency is considered as part of a composite indicator of organizational performance by Andrews et al. All the articles consider measures of service outcomes and include managerial effectiveness, productivity (Brewer; Chun and Rainey), and formal effectiveness (Andrews et al.; Hill; Martin and Smith; Pitts). Measures of responsiveness figure in two articles—Chun and Rainey examine customer service orientation, and Andrews et al. include citizen satisfaction and consumer satisfaction.

t: How Does Public Management Affect Government Performance? Findings from International Research
abs: Despite the growing importance of public management reform around the world, relatively little scholarship evaluates the contributions of public management to government performance, that is, to the character and consequences of service provision by public agencies. One study (Hill and Lynn 2005) evaluated over eight hundred American empirical studies that address issues of public management effectiveness in a wide variety of fields, subfields, and disciplines. In this article we employ the analytic framework of Hill and Lynn—a polycentric “logic of governance”—to evaluate 193 research articles published in English that use non-American, or what we will term international, empirical evidence. Our evaluation reveals more similarities in American and non-American public management research, and in the determinants of government performance, than one might expect, given the distinctiveness of the American politico-administrative system. These similarities may be deceptive, however. International investigators exhibit somewhat different modeling strategies, tending, for example, to favor more linear managerialist hypotheses—changes in structure lead to changes outcomes, for example—than American research, which is more concerned with intragovernmental complexities. The fact that the use of a polycentric logic of governance revealed highly suggestive similarities and differences in the determinants of performance in public organizations suggests the potential value of this kind of analytic strategy in both single investigations and in meta-analyses of public management reform.

t: The Effects of Managerial Succession on Organizational Performance
abs: Boyne and Dahya (2002) posit that the means, motives, and opportunities available to top managers will affect their ability to impact organizational performance. In this analysis, I test the theory posited by Boyne and Dahya and expand the model by exploring whether the performance effects of executive succession differ between an internal promotion and an external hire. Using Texas school superintendents as the managers in question, I use pooled, time-series data to test both the immediate and the long-term effects of managerial succession on performance. The findings reveal that an immediate, negative effect of executive succession is present only in the case of an externally hired replacement and that the long-term effect of managerial change on organizational performance is positive. These findings suggest that public managerial succession does influence organizational performance.

t: “Walking the Walk” of Public Service Motivation: Public Employees and Charitable Gifts of Time, Blood, and Money
abs: Research generally indicates that public employees “talk the talk,” but do they also “walk the walk” of the public service motive (PSM)? Are public service employees more likely than others to engage in public service activities? The behavioral implications of PSM are addressed by studying the involvement in charitable activities of public, nonprofit, and private workers. Using data from the 2002 General Social Survey, multivariate logistic regression models are estimated to examine self-reported gifts of time, blood, and money to charitable organizations. It is found that government employees are more likely to volunteer for charity and to donate blood than for-profit employees are. Additionally, nonprofit workers are also more likely than their for-profit counterparts to volunteer. However, no difference is found among public service and private employees in terms of individual philanthropy. These findings generally lend support for the hypothesis that PSM is more prominent in public service than in private organizations, especially as it pertains to government personnel.
